The Doce Fire (pronounced Dough-see) was reported at 1130 AM on June 18. Dry and breezy to windy conditions lasted from June 18 through June 24.  This pushed the fire to the northeast over the Granite Mountains.  The fire grew to 6,767 by June 24.  During the peak staffing there were 650 personnel including: 16 hand crews, 22 engines, 5 water tenders, 2 dozers, and 4 helicopters.  The firefighting cost was $6.9 million by the end of June. Only one minor injury was reported.
The Doce Fire started in June and was 100% contained on July 12 at 1800 at 6,767 acres.  Total cost to fire the fire was around $7.4 million with $6.9 million spent in June.

The Yarnell Hill Fire was started by lightning around 536 PM on Friday June 28 about 3.5 miles west of Yarnell. The fire grew to about 6 acres by Saturday morning. Strong outflow winds form a thunderstorm northeast of Prescott hit the fire Sunday afternoon. The wind caused the fire to blow up and it overtook 19 Granite Mountain Hot Shots. They all perished. The fire grew to around 8,300 acres by the end of June (the final size was 8,400 acres). The Yavapai County Sheriff's Office said that 127 buildings in Yarnell and two in Peeples Valley were destroyed in the fire. ||Officials shut down 25 miles of Arizona State Route 89 shortly after the fire started. All of Yarnell was evacuated and part of Peeples Valley was evacuated (at least 600 people total). The Red Cross said that 351 people spent at least one night at one of their shelters. ||A Type 2 incident management team was in charge of the fire late on June 30, with a Type 1 team ordered. Southwest Area Type 1 IMT assumed management of the fire on July 1. ||Resources on June 30 included 16 engines, eight water tenders, two crash-rescue vehicles, two structure protection vehicles, one bulldozer, one hotshot crew (with another four on order), seven Type 2 handcrews, a camp crew, and four Type 2 hand crews on order. One very large airtanker (VLAT) and an air attack unit were also on order.

The Yarnell Hill Fire was started by lightning around 536 PM on Friday June 28 about 3.5 miles west of Yarnell. The fire grew to around 8,300 acres by the end of June (the final size was 8,400 acres). The Yavapai County Sheriff's Office said that 127 buildings in Yarnell and two in Peeples Valley were destroyed in the fire. All of Yarnell was evacuated and part of Peeples Valley was evacuated (at least 600 people total).  A Type 2 incident management team was in charge of the fire late on June 30, with a Type 1 team ordered. Southwest Area Type 1 IMT assumed management of the fire on July 1.  By the morning of July 2 the fire had grown another 800 acres, as mapped by an infrared aircraft flight. The fire was still at zero containment. Resources included five Type 1 hotshot crews, seven Type 2 crews, three Type 1 heavy helicopters, two Type 2 medium helicopters, two Type 3 light helicopters, and 36 engines.
Hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter was reported in University Heights south to Kachina Village. The Turkey Butte fire lookout tower suffered broken windows due to the hail.
Heavy Rain Fell across Flagstaff. 1.10 inches of rain fell at a NWS employee's house.  Street flooding was reported and several intersections had water one to two feet deep.
Strong winds from a thunderstorm snapped a large (3.5 food diameter) cottonwood tree in half in Cornville.  A fence was also blown down.
Spotters in Heber-Overgaard reported from 0.48 inches of rain to 1.40 inches of rain in as little as 25 minutes. Hail up to 1/2 inch in diameter and wind gusts to 48 MPH was also reported.
A high based thunderstorm produced wind gusts to 60 MPH in St Johns.
Heavy rain caused County Road 1126 near Greer to be come impassible due to heavy runoff.  The report was received at 655 PM MST.
A trained spotter reported one inch diameter hail with heavy rain and localized flooding in Heber-Overgaard.
Up to two inches of rain was reported in Pinetop-Lakeside.  Dime sized hail covered the ground.
Very heavy rain (2.50 inches) caused water to flow across roads and several were barricaded.  A few homes in Camp Verde estates were flooded.

Heavy rain over the east side of Mt Elden and part of the Schultz Fire scar lead to water and debris flowing over residential roads and Highway 89.  Water entered several trailers and knocked down a slump block wall around the trailer park. Road crews had to clear the debris off the roads. Law enforcement reported widespread flooding from the Flagstaff Mall to Silver Saddle Road/Highway 89.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm cause water to flow over several roads in Yarnell.  There was significant flows through the drainages.
Heavy rain over the Canyon De Chelly National Monument caused flash flooding in Pueblo Co Wash.  The water was snapping trees along the banks of the wash.
About 2.50 inches of rain fell in about 90 minutes.
One inch diameter hail fell with 0.38 inches of rain in just 10 minutes.
About 1.28 inches of rain fell in just 45 minutes ten miles south of Mayer.
A river guide was struck by lightning while on a river trip in the Grand Canyon.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms produced flash flooding in far east Flagstaff. Water was covering Highway 89 at Silver Saddle and Campbell Avenue. Water was also flooding trailer park homes.
Two inches of rain fell in less than an hour in Alpine. Two to three inches of water covered the intersection of Highways 180 and 191.
Lightning struck three people at LeFavre Scenic Overlook along Highway 89 about eight miles north of Jacobs Lake. Two people died and the third person sustained non-life-threatening injuries.
Heavy rain (1.75 inch) produced minor amounts water and rock across area roads in Whiteriver from runoff below the Locus Fire scar.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms produced flowing water across several roads from Campbell Avenue southward below the southern half of the Schultz Fire Scar. Water was also flowing across Silver Saddle Road near Mary's Drive. A rain gauge in the area measured 1.69 inches of rain.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms produced flooding on roads in east Flagstaff. Some roads became impassable...including historic Route 66 for about 20 minutes. Flood waters entered 15 to 20 homes. About 2.25 inches of rain fell between 11 AM and 1 PM on Fanning Drive below the Pipeline Trail.
Heavy rain fell over the hills north of West Route 66. The runoff caused damage to 5 properties between 130 PM and 200 PM.
One inch diameter hail fell in east Flagstaff along with very heavy rain.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused 2.5 feet of water from Granite Creek to flow over Highway 89 near Granite Gardens Drive. A water rescue was performed.

Heavy rain from a thunderstorm created a large wall of water that carried large boulders and debris through Indian Gardens below the South Rim of the Grand Canyon. Trails were washed out. The water was estimated to be 8 to 10 feet deep in places. Campers were trapped in the Indian Gardens Campground during the flooding.  The peak of the flooding was at 300 PM.
O'Leary Peak received 1.88 inches of rain in 45 minutes at the fire lookout. Pea sized hail covered the ground half an inch deep.
Flood water and debris closed the main road in Dilkon for an hour.
Heavy rain (2.25 inches) from a thunderstorm fell in Fort Valley.  Hail 1/4 inch in diameter also fell during the thunderstorm.
Heavy rain over the Yarnell Hill Fire scar caused flash flooding in the town of Yarnell. A couple roads were over topped and debris flows ere observed.
Flood waters flowed over the bridge over Silver Creek on Bourden Ranch Road northeast of Show Low.
Heavy rain flooded the intersection of Cottage and Leroux near downtown Flagstaff.

Very heavy rain, up to four inches in two hours, fell in and around Ash Fork with flash flooding.  Interstate 40 was closed from mile marker 140 to 144 for two and a half hours because of all the water and debris on the roadway.  Five inches to a foot of standing water was reported in business on the west side of town. Double Ranch Road was under water. Flooding was reported in the Kaibab Subdivision.  The flooding in Ash Fork was slowly receding by 945 PM. The flood waters Ash Fork flowed down Ash Fork Draw, Partridge Creek and into Big Chino Wash all the way down to near Paulden.
Heavy rain a few miles upstream from Havasu Village caused flooding of Havasu Creek.
Two inches of rain caused street flooding in Shumway.
Flash flooding out of Upper Antelope Canyon closed Highway 98 east of Page. Several thunderstorms formed over the Antelope Canyon drainage though the afternoon and continued the flooding.

Thunderstorms produced flooding in Garden Creek along the popular Bright Angel Trail. The depth of the flood waters through Indian Gardens was 3 to 5 feet deep. The first flash flood on Garden Creek was reported at 1238 PM MST.
Flash flooding caused Havasu Creek to rise 5 feet through the Village of Supai.  Minor damage was reported.
Other thunderstorms caused a second flash flood on Garden Creek at 342 PM MST.
Flash flooding was reported in Antelope Canyon southeast of Page. Eight to 12 inches of new sand was deposited in this popular slot canyon.

A major flash flood hit Antelope Canyon with water hitting the underside of a bridge. The water in the normally dry slot canyon is over 40 feet in places. Flood waters in Honey Draw were running over State Route 99 and and State Highway 89.  The water and mud flowed down State Highway 89 and into a gas station at Lake Powell Boulevard. The mud that was deposited in the parking lot was 12-18 inches deep and trapped vehicles.
A 1 to 2 foot rise on Cibecue Creek was reported near Cibecue.  A five foot rise was reported on a stream gauge downstream of Cibecue. The drainage area was burned in 2002 in the Rodeo-Chediski Fire.

Flood water entered a home on Cosnino Road. Flooding was also reported on Wapiti and Casnino Road.  About half a foot of water covered Towsend-Winona Road about half a mile west of the Interstate 40 junction.
Heavy rain fell over the Brins Fire scar (2006) in Oak Creek Canyon. This caused a flash flood and rock slide that blocked Highway 89A near mile post 378.
One inch diameter hail covered the roadway on I-40 at mile marker 227 about 25 miles east of Flagstaff.
Portions of Rincon Road were closed along Martinez Wash due to flash flooding.
Flash flooding was reported along Highway 191 between mile markers 322 and 324.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm produced flash flooding along Indian Creek in Indian Gardens. Minor damage was reported.

Heavy rain from a thunderstorm produced a flash flood in Deer Creek. The flood was big enough to move boulders downstream. Fifteen rafters were trapped by the flood and were unable to return to their camp until the flooding ended.
One inch diameter hail was reported in Kachina Village.
Heavy rain caused street flooding in Winslow. Up to three feet of water had collected in low lying spots.
A weather spotter one mile north of McNary reported 1.61 inches of rain between noon and 445 PM.
Heavy rain caused minor driveway damage in McCann Estates on the northeast side of Flagstaff.
A spotter on the north side of Payson reported 1.25 inches of rain.
One inch of rain fell in 45 minutes near Hutch Mountain.

Heavy rain caused at least four inches of rain along Highway 89 from Fanning to Townsend-Winona near the Flagstaff Mall. Water was running in all normally dry washes from McCann Estates to Campbell Road below the Radio Fire (1977) and the Schultz Fire (2010).  A few roads in that area had minor amounts of water flowing over them. Soliere was flooded between Country Club Drive and 4th Street and was closed. Later in the evening (753-808 PM), 1/3 of an inch fell in just 15 minutes in Kachina Village.
Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch rose 2 feet in a flash flood late in the evening.
A rapid rise on Havasu Creek was observed on the gauge...from 14 feet to 17.3 feet with minor flooding.
Severe flooding was reported in Round Valley. One vehicle was stuck in a flooded wash and one of the roads into Middle Round Valley was impassable.
Constellation Road north of Wcikenburg was washed out.
A spotter measured 2.20 inches of rain overnight. Other locations in and around Sedona measured 1.85 inches.
Numerous trees up to 14 inches in diameter were knocked down by thunderstorm winds.
A spotter in Star Valley reported 0.97.
A trained spotter in Tonto Village reported 1.30 inches of rain. Forest Road 64 into Tonto Village remained open.
Heavy rain (estimated 3 inches) caused large rocks and debris to fall on Highway 89 about 8 miles west of Jerome.
The funnel cloud started as a large bowl shaped cloud, lowered, and then sharpened into a tight funnel and then dissipated.
State Highway 260 was temporarily closed because there was too much water on the roadway.

Crown King Road was damaged by water over topping the road between mile posts 15 and 19 near Mulddoon Gulch.  Dual Pole Radar estimated around 2.50 inches of rain had fallen in that area. This area was impacted by the Gladiator Fire in 2012.
Interstate 17 was closed 3 miles north of Black Canyon City after heavy rain knocked rocks and debris on the roadway.

A stream gauge on Kanab Creek north of the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon reported a ten foot rise to 9,500 CFS.  The Colorado River often fluctuates around this flow in this part of the Grand Canyon.
Heavy rain caused street flooding on Cedar St and 4th Street.  The water as a foot deep in places.
A 54 year old man was walking along the south edge of Scott Reservoir with two other people when he was stuck and killed by lightning.
Cottonwood-Tuzigoot tied the record high of 107 for the day last set in 1996.
The Prescott Airport tied the record high of 97 for the day last set in 1996.  The airport is at 5052 feet above sea level.
The Flagstaff Airport reached a high of 91 which broke the record high of 89 for the day last set in 1985. The Flagstaff Airport is at an elevation of 7003 feet above sea level.
The Page Airport set a new high temperature of 104 for the day. This broke the old record of 99 last set in 2010. Page is at an elevation of 4310 feet above sea level.

Forest Road 514 was washed out and was impassible about 1/3 of a mile west of Highway 89.  Radar estimated that 1.75 inches of rain fell in that area.

Two inches of rain fell in half an hour near Williamson Vally road just north of Prescott. There was four feet of water in the normally dry wash. Logs and cars were carried off of roads. A flash flood in Prescott carried a car down a flooded stream.  A swift water rescue successfully recovered the occupants.
Law Enforcement reported flooding along Road Five North in Chino Valley. A woman wading downstream in Granite Creek was washed away by flood waters. Her body was found later that day.

Thunderstorms produced about one inch of rain in under an hour. This created some flooding problems in the Grand Canyon Village and below the Rim. One range guage in the area reported 0.92 inches of rain in 40 minutes. Another guage in the area reported 1.85 inches of rain between 135 PM and 245 PM.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused flash flooding and trail damage on the Bright Angel Trail at Garden Creek below Indian Gardens.  Flooding covered an intersection at the South Rim by one foot of mud. The basement of the Park Headquarters flooded.
Heavy rain caused urban street flooding with reports of water and mud on South Milton Road.

A three foot rise on Havasu Creek was reported at 253 PM.  Later, at just after 400 PM, Supai Police reported that trails had been flooded and washed out.  One bridge was flooded and parts of the Village of Supai were flooded.

Heavy rain flooded some low water crossings in the Payson area. Radar estimated that 1.00 to 1.24 inches of rain fell between 145 and 230 PM MST.  A weather spotter reported 1.75 inches of rain during the day.
Businesses were flooded at the junction of Highway 191 and Hospital Drive.  Flooding was also reported on Highway 191 at mile post 446.8.
Heavy rain over the Yarnell Hill Fire scar produced flash flooding in the town of Yarnell. Water was flowing over the roads near the junction of Willow and Stahl.
Water from an earthen dam caused flooding of several residences and mobile homes at 200 PM near US Highway 191 at mile post 467.2.  The dam broke around noon.
A box culvert was overcome by flood water near mile post 417 on Highway 160. Several local residences and the Chapter House were flooded.
One inch diameter hail was reported 3 miles east of Whiteriver.
Flooding and debris was reported on several area roads. Three homes were flooded in East Fork and one in Sevenmile. The amount of damage was unknown.
Heavy rain caused street flooding (curb to curb) in Taylor.  Water was also flowing between homes and creating trenches.
A thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud  about 6 miles east of Mormon Lake.
Heavy rain produced flash flooding on Highway 160 near mile post 408 and on Highway 163 near mile post 400.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding over Highway 191 near mile post 497.
The peak wind gust measured at the Flagstaff Airport ASOS was 64 MPH at 312 PM. The winds gusted above 50 MPH for several hours.
Heavy rain caused flooding across the Navajo Nation. Road damage from flooding prevented travel in Red Valley. Water entered a store, roads were damaged, and bridge was damaged in Mexican Water.
Fifteen sheep were killed by lightning.  Time and location are estimates.
Close to 50 families were displace across the Navajo Nation in Apache County because of the flash flooding. Part of the Navajo Zoo was inundated with water.

The ASOS at the Show Low Airport recorded a peak wind gust of 60 MPH.

Heavy snow began falling around 900 AM with 8 inches accumulating by 500 PM with white-out conditions continuing. Two more inches fell by early morning on the 24th for a storm total of 10 inches.
Seven inches of snow fell between 400 AM and 2 PM.  Another 3 inches of snow fell between 2 PM and 9 PM.
A man was stuck and killed by lightning while fishing from a canoe on Big Lake.
Ten to 12 inches of snow fell in and around Jacob Lake.

A band of heavy snow developed over the western portions of the Western Mogollon Rim during the evening and persisted through the night. Fifteen inches of snow fell at the NWS office in Bellemont. Twelve inches of snow fell just outside of Parks. Arizona Snowbowl reported 8 to 12 inches (9,200 and 10,800 feet elevation).
A band of heavy snow developed over western portions of the Eastern Mogollon Rim in the evening and persisted through the night. Ten inches of snow fell at the Happy Jack Ranger Station.
The Flagstaff Airport set a record low of -9F. The previous record of -8F was last set in 1951. Bellemont set a record low of -14F. The previous record of -9F was last set in 2009.
The Grand Canyon Airport set a record low of -23F. The previous record of -15F was last set in 2009.
Bagdad tied the record low of 20F. The previous 20F was last seen in 1972.

About two inches of snow fell across the Western Mogollon Rim starting on the last day of January. There had been no precipitation in the area for 39 days. The fresh snow caused a number of traffic accidents. Department of Public Safety responded to 10 collisions on I-17 and I-40 by 4 PM. Only one person had injuries in those crashes. Flagstaff Police Department responded to 16 crashes--two involved injuries. Coconino County Sheriff's Department responded to 7 crashes and five slide offs. A crash on southbound I-17 near Munds Park forced the closure of the Highway for an hour.
Snow was falling at the time of a fatal car and truck collision on Highway 64 in the Grand Canyon National Park.  The two other people in the car were injured.
The ASOS at the Grand Canyon Airport reported a peak wind gust of 58 MPH at just after 100 PM MST.
The ASOS at the Flagstaff Airport reported a peak wind gust of 59 MPH at 213 PM MST.

A rancher was burning weeds and the fire escaped due to windy and abnormally dry conditions. The fire grew to 100 acres and threatened several homes.  The Prescott Airport just 20 miles away had only received 0.02 inches of rain in the prior 7 weeks.  Average amount for this time period is over 2.50 inches.

The Slide Fire started in Oak Creek Canyon and quickly burned north and west out of the canyon onto the Western Mogollon Rim. The fire eventually burned over 22,000 acres in Oak Creek Canyon, West Fork Oak Creek Canyon, and parts of the rim country bordering the canyons. The fire stayed west of Oak Creek and Highway 89A that connects Sedona and Flagstaff. The total fire fighting cost was over $7 million. The cost of rehabilitation and the expected flood damage has yet to be determined.

Heavy snow (over 80 inches in 10 days) caused a large avalanche in the San Fransisco Peaks just north of Flagstaff. The top of the wide avalanche started along a north-south ridge and and continued to an east-west ridge. The headwall was an estimated half mile wide. The avalanche dropped between 500 and 800 feet. The avalanche was in a wilderness area where there are no structures. Other avalanches also occurred during and after this storm as a result of the heavy snow and thaw cycles. Pinpointing the time of the avalanches is difficult. Avalanches were also reported in Abineau Canyon, Fremont Peak, and Doyle peak. Some of these slides toppled trees that were 24 inches in diameter.

Some of the storm total snow amounts (in inches) include: Snowbowl (10,800') 26.0, Bellemont 10.7,  Flagstaff Airport 6.9, Williams 3.0, and Doney Park 2.0.  Flagstaff Police Department reported only six accidents in the City limits. However, The  Arizona Department of Public Safety responded to 24 collisions and 40 slide-offs in the Flagstaff area. Six of collisions resulted in injuries. One accident injured two people who were taken to the hospital, where they were treated, and released.

Five roads were closed in Chino Valley because of flash flooding. A vehicle was stranded at Road 5 North and Reed Road. The fire department was able to rescue the occupants and a tow truck pulled the vehicle out.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain south and southeast of Bagdag. Spotter estimated that between an inch and a inch and a half of rain fell over the area.  Low water crossings on Highways 96 and 87 had between 6 and 8 inches of water flowing across them. The roads remained open.

The Nazlini Wash flooded low water crossings.
A thunderstorm produced heavy rain north of Kayenta. Police reported water of Highway 163 at Mile Post 400.
A thunderstorm produce heavy rain and a flash flood in de Chelly Wash. There was one fatality when a truck overturned in the flooded wash around 700 PM MDT.
Winslow Police confirmed that a brick wall collapsed from strong thunderstorm winds. The Winslow ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 53 MPH at 339 PM MST.

Heavy rain south of Winslow caused flash flooding. A car got stuck in the flood waters seven miles south of Winslow on SR 99. Flash flooding also restricted SR 99 to just one lane about 1 mile south of Winslow.
A funnel cloud was seen from Many Farms. It reached about halfway to the ground then dissipated.

Very heavy rain fell over the Marble Canyon area from near Navajo Bridge to near Jacob Lake. Up to five feet of was was flowing over Highway 89 in places. Significant mud, debris, and truck sized boulders washed onto the roads.  Highway 89 was closed for 24 miles while road crews could clean debris off the road. Some of the boulders had to be blasted before they could be moved because they were so large. The flash flood even changed Soap Creek Rapid on the Colorado River in Marble Canyon (upstream from the Grand Canyon) making it more difficult for river runners to navigate the rapid.
A trained spotter estimated that winds were gusting to 65 MPH along SR 89A in Marble Canyon. Time was estimated using radar imagery.
A maintenance worker at the Lake Powell Tribal Park reported significant flooding in Antelope Canyon. Time estimated using radar data.
Several trees were blown down in Prescott Valley along Addis Avenue from Viewpoint to near Rockland Drive. The trees ranged from 1 to 2 feet in diameter.
High winds blew through the central portion of the city with downed trees and downed power lines.
Flash flooding washed out the majority of the dirt roads in the Dilkon, Tees Toh, Indian Wells, to White Cone area.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused flash flooding along Highway 160 between MP 361 and MP 379. The flooding stopped traffic.
Heavy rain produced flash flooding in Indian Route 59 at MP 22 and MP 33.
Water flooded the road near the junction of Highway 160 and State Route 98.
The river gauge on the Moenkopi Wash near Tuba City jumped from near zero to 6,900 CFS in under 30 minutes. NWS personnel confirmed that the water was encouraging homes in the community of Moenkopi.

Between one and 1.25 inches of rain fell across the Doney Park area of far northeast Flagstaff in under 50 minutes.  The power was also knocked out by the storm. Wind gusts to 45 MPH and half inch hail was also reported.

The Rimrock Fire District reported wind caused roof damage to homes along Airport Road, one mobile home flipped, and 12 inch diameter trees were uprooted. A dust devil damaged a dog run and the roof of a house. The large dog run was thrown approximately 60 feet.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Yarnell with brief heavy rain.

A thunderstorm produced between 0.50 and 1.25 inches of rain over the Juniper Fire scar. Debris flows closed Highway 288 at MP 277 at Pocket Creek. Reynolds Creek washed out the highway at MP 286. There was a minor washout on Cherry Creek Road.
A confirmed gustnado was on the ground for approximately 4 minutes.
The Tenderfoot fire was human caused and started about a mile south Yarnell. Strong southwest winds pushed the fire to the northeast and east of Yarnell in chaparral and grass.

The lightning caused Wildcat Fire burned around 1,500 acres on the eastern slopes of the Kaibab Plateau. Strong southwest winds pushed the fire northeastward and away from Highway 67. This highway is the only paved road that provides access to the North Rim of the Grand Canyon. This fire caused the closure of several trails in the area.

Lightning started the Jack Fire near Happy Jack in a ponderosa forest on May 29 around 115 PM. This ecosystem is fire adapted and the fire was allowed to burn within a set boundary. The fire burned about 500 acres in May and reached a final size of 33,850 acres by June 24 when progression stopped.

Lightning started the Jack Fire near Happy Jack in a ponderosa forest on May 29 around 115 PM. This ecosystem is fire adapted and the fire was allowed to burn within a set boundary. The fire burned about 33,350 acres in June and reached 33, 850 acres by June 24 when progression stopped.

The Cedar Fire started southwest of Show Low on June 15th. The fire burned north, northeast, and east for three days for a total of about 13,000 acres. Then, on June 19th, strong northeast winds caused the fire to jump containment lines and burn 14,000 acres in one day. This also was one of the hottest days on record with highs 10-15 degrees above average for the day. The total size by June 27 was about 46,000 acres.

The Cedar Fire started southwest of Show Low on June 15th in Navajo County. The fire burned north-northeast, and east for three days for a total of about 13,000 acres. Then, on June 19th, strong northeast winds caused the fire to jump containment lines and burn 14,000 acres in one day and into Gila County. This also was one of the hottest days on record with highs 10-15 degrees above average for the day. The total size by June 27 was about 46,000 acres.
The Juniper Fire started about 10 miles south of Young on May 20th in ponderosa pine, mixed conifer, and oak shrub. By the end of May, the fire burned about 7,800 acres.
The Juniper Fire started about 10 miles south of Young on May 20th in ponderosa pine, mixed conifer, and oak shrub. The fire burned about 22,800 acres in June for a total of  30,600 acres by June 14.

The Bert Fire was started by lighting on May 29 near Highway 180 about 10 miles southeast of Valle. This natural fire was allowed to burn in a fire adapted ecosystem. The fire burned about 5800 acres in June and bout 200 acres in May.

A record high of 87 degrees was set at the Flagstaff airport. The previous record was 86 set for this date was 86 set in 1996.

Radar estimated that 0.5 to 1.2 inches of rain fell over the Cedar Fire scar. A 12 to 18 inch crest moved down Cedar Creek and through the town of Cedar Creek. This is the first of many post fire floods that happened during the summer of 2016.
Radar estimated 2 inches of rain storm total.  The Sheriff Office reported water up to car door in downtown and south of downtown. Pea and dime sized hail was also reported with this storm.
The Page ASOS reported a peak wind gust 59 MPH from a thunderstorm.

Radar estimated 1.50 to 2.50 inches of rain over the central part of the Cedar Fire scar starting around 530 PM MST. A 4 to 5 foot flood crest reached the Highway 73 bridge at the town of Cedar Creek at 720 PM MST.
Flash flood debris reached the Arizona Department of Transportation yard near  Workman Creek. The flow included large boulders, deep mud, and debris from recent fire activity.
Heavy rain and hail up to 1/2 inch in diameter caused local flooding in and around Williams.
Heavy rain and dime sized (0.70 inch diameter) caused flowing water in area washes/road crossings.
An inch and a half of rain caused Big Bug Creek to flow about 2 feet from the top of the bridge.

The Fuller Fire started with a lightning bolt near Fuller Canyon on the North Rim of the Grand Canyon near Cape Royal Road. Fire is a natural part of the ecosystem on the Kiabab Plateau so this fire was managed for resource benefit. The fire grew to 9 acres by July 10.

The Fuller Fire started with a lightning bolt near Fuller Canyon on the North Rim of the Grand Canyon near Cape Royal Road. Fire is a natural part of the ecosystem on the Kiabab Plateau so this fire was managed for resource benefit. The fire grew to 9 acres by July 10. Then southwest winds pushed the fire northeast with active spotting. Southwest winds continued to increase through July 15 (4.5 mile run) with the greatest spread on the 16th as the fire burned out large bowls and side canyons filling in unburned areas. The fire was 14,385 acres by July 23. By August 14th, the fire had slowly reached 14,541 acres.

Martinez Wash rose 5.7 feet in less than an hour.

A NWS employee reported 1.46 inches of rain.
The Flagstaff Airport reported 1.25 inches of rain in 57 minutes and a total of 1.33 inches of rain in 90 minutes.
A video showed that the Tanner Wash was flowing under the Highway 89 bridge. Rainfall amount was estimated from radar to be around 2.00 inches.
Two to three feet of water covered roads that crossed Black Canyon Creek.
A cold core funnel cloud was seen as far away as Gallup, New Mexico.
Granite Creek rose 3.5 feet near Prescott with a peak flow of 1468 CFS. An upstream gauge rose 4 feet with a peak flow of 1209 CFS.
Thunderstorms produced 1.42 inches of rain over about 2 hours. Minor street flooding and flowing washes were reported.
A funnel cloud was seen about two miles south-southwest of Williams.
Heavy rain caused the Paria River at Lees Ferry to rise 4 feet.

Trained spotters reported one half inch to one inch diameter hail covering the ground between 2 and 8 miles north of Show Low.
A funnel cloud was seen from Joseph City.
The snow total for this 72 hour event was between 6 and 8.5 inches in the Forest Lakes area.

Ten inches of snow was reported at 10,800 feet above mean sea level. Four to 6 inches of snow was reported around Williams and Flagstaff areas. Eight inches of snow was reported in Munds Park. The heaviest snow fell late afternoon and early evening on Sunday--a very heavy travel day after Thanksgiving and again Monday afternoon and evening. Area law enforcement officials reported the following with this event: 177 crashes and motorist assists (7 injuries) for Arizona Highway Patrol, 83 crashes (10 injuries) for Flagstaff Police, 28 crashes and motorist assist for Coconino County Sheriff, 5 crashes for Northern Arizona University Police.  Interstate 17 from Flagstaff to Phoenix was blocked for periods of time because of wrecks and road conditions. There were also wrecks on Interstate 40, Highway 180, and Highway 89.
A trained spotter in Forest Lakes reported 3.89 inches of rain (some melted snow) from just before midnight on the 16th to 900 AM on December 17.

The ASOS at the Flagstaff Airport reported wind gusts at times over 58 MPH from around 730 PM until midnight. The highest wind gust was 64 MPH around 1000 PM and 1100 PM. At least one wood fence sustained major damage when about 4 eight foot sections blew down on the northwest side of town. Arizona Snowbowl (a local ski area) reported that 300 trees blew down across their area (777 acres in the San Fransisco Peaks). They also reported power outages.

A weather spotter reported 1.78 inches of rain in Forest Lakes.

Heavy rain caused significant rise on Dry Beaver Creek (the creek jumped from 43 CFS to 1,030 CFS in 15 minutes (2.84 feet to 4.65 feet) starting at 815 AM MST.  A swift water rescue was preformed where East Kimberly's Way crosses Dry Beaver Creek at a low water crossing (215 PM MST on the 22nd). The creek crested at 2,310 CFS (5.78 feet--almost a 3 foot rise) at 215 PM MST on the 22nd.

Heavy rain caused Oak Creek to flood. The lower end of Doodlebug Road was impassible. The gauge on Oak Creek at Sedona (Tlaquepaque) started to show an increase in flow just after midnight on the 21st.  By 930 AM on th2 21st, the creek had risen 4 feet and some of the low water crossings were closed. The base flow is at 2.43 feet and 43 CFS. There were several crests as different drainages emptied into the main creek. The peak flow was 7.68 feet (4,330 CFS) at 545 AM MST on the 23rd.  The crest moved down past the Cornville gauge at 1000 AM MST on the 23rd at 3,730 CFS.

The Bear Fire started about ten miles southeast of Clints Well in Bear Canyon. It eventually merged with the Highline Fire and continued to grow until around July 7.  Together, the fires burned 9789 acres.
The Highline Fire started on June 10 about 8 miles north of Payson.  The fire eventually merged with the Bear Fire and, together, burned 9780 acres by July 7.
The Highline Fire started in June and was considered contained by 1800 on July 7.  The Bear Fire and Highline Fire merged to become the Highline Fire.

The Brooklyn, Bull, and Cedar Fires were all caused by lighting about 6 miles north through northeast of Black Canyon City. In all, around 33,600 acres of tall grass, shrubs, and juniper trees burned. There were no structures threatened. Around 110 firefighting personnel were involved in this incident. The fire was low intensity for this vegetation type so the threat of post fire flooding was minimal.

The Boundary Fire burned through 17,788 acres in the Kendrick Mountain Wilderness. This was a lightning caused fire. An indirect suppression strategy was implemented due to the significant safety concerns of putting fire personnel in certain areas on the mountain. Structures near the top of the mountain (including a fire lookout tower and an historic cabin) were successfully saved.  The fire burned through timber and litter in understory, short grass, and heavy logging slash. There was also heavy down and dead debris from Pumpkin Fire in 2000.

A thunderstorm produced 1.13 inches of rain in about 25 minutes.
More than an inch of rain fell in 25 minutes at the Prescott Courthouse.
A thunderstorm produced 1.50 inches of rain in just 30 minutes in Nutrioso.
A thunderstorm produced 0.64 inches of rain from 812 PM to 8:45 PM.  At 8:22 PM, the rainfall rate was 6.0 inches an hour.
Thunderstorms produced 0.93 inches of rain from 1600 to 1830. The maximum rainfall rate was 3.6 inches an hour.
Thunderstorms produced 1.36 inches of rain in 30 minutes in Payson.
The flow in Bonita Creek increased as a result of heavy rain on the Highline Fire scar. The water remained within banks and did not impact the homes in the area.
Cedar Creek was flowing at a gauge height of 8 feet at the bridge on Highway 73 at 1600.

A thunderstorm produced half to three-quarters of an inch of rain in 15 minutes, minor street flooding, peak sized hail, and 50 MPH wind gusts. Small (less than two inches in diameter) tree branches were blown down. Brawshaw Middle School reported 1.20 inches of rain.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar. This caused dangerously high flows in Grapevine Creek. Central Avenue in Mayer was closed at Big Bug Creek because of flooding, mud, and debris over the roadway. About two feet of debris flow was observed in the creek which had been previously dry.
Heavy rain over the Brooklyn Fire scar caused flash flooding in Black Canyon Creek. The water was flowing black from ash in the normally dry riverbed.
Heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar caused a debris flow across Forest Road 67.
Winds from a thunderstorm knocked power poles down along Castle Creek north of Lake Pleasant.

Very heavy rain over the Highland Fire scar and surrounding areas produced flash flooding in Ellison Creek which flows into the East Verde River. This is a very popular swimming area during the summer. Ten people were killed by the flooding (ages 2 to 57). Four people were rescued by helicopter after they were trapped in trees.
Yavapai Flood Control reported that Fain Lake was overflowing causing flooding in Lynx Creek.
One inch diameter hail was reported in Payson via social media. Time was estimated using radar.
Pine trees were bend over sideways. There was also damage to manzanita and scrub oak trees.
A thunderstorm produced high winds gusts (estimated at 60 MPH). The storm also produced pea sized hail and fog with visibility of 1/4 mile or less.
Thunderstorms produced wind gusts to 60 MPH.
A peak wind gust of 67 MPH was measured at the Humbug Creek RAWS (estimated time).
Lightning struck and injured seven military personnel while they were working on a grounded helicopter on Camp Navajo Army Depot.  All seven were treated and released.
Flash flooding was reported on Scott Wash over State Route 377 between mile marker 7 and 8.
Thunderstorms produced one to 1.5 inch diameter hail west to southwest of Prescott.
Strong winds pushed a traveling Jeep off the road and it ran into a tree.
Golf ball sized (1 3/4 inch diameter) hail fell 5 miles north of Iron Springs Road on Williamson Valley Road.
Big Chino Wash rose 3 feet in a short time at Highway 89.
Russell Wash was flooding in Lake Montezuma.
Power lines and trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds in Bagdad.
Strong winds from a thunderstorm tore a 24 foot by 72 foot metal roof off a shed. It tore the (metal) sheets off like paper, split/broke the 2X6s (wood rafters).  Winds estimated at 50 to 55 MPH.

A flash flood was reported in Walker Creek, a tributary into Wet Beaver Creek, at 845 PM. The water was estimated to be flowing 4-5 feet deep in a normally dry area. Radar showed that two inches of rain fell southeast of the area an hour to an hour and a half earlier.
The river gauge on the Agua Fria River at Humbuldt showed a rapid 4 foot rise. This was below the Goodwin Fire scar.
Law enforcement reported flooded roadway at Freeman Hollow.  The road was closed and manhole covers were lifted off due to the force of the water. Flood waters entered properties.
Law enforcement reported boulders on Highway 89A with flooded roadways in Oak Creek Canyon.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms flooded Willow Creek Road and Commerce Road in the Prescott area. One truck was stuck in the flood water. Three feet of water and debris covered Emerald Road in Diamond Valley Subdivision.  There was at least a two foot rise in Alberson Wash upstream from Fain Lake and Lynx Creek.

Thunderstorms produce heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar.  This lead to flash flooding in Big Big Bug Creek and Grapevine Creek which both flow into the Agua Fria River. This lead to a double crest in the flash flood downstream. The flooding started around 1745 in Mayer and 1845 in Spring Valley. People were evacuated in Mayer.  The stream gauge on Agua Fria River near Mayer showed a 5.84 foot rise in 45 minutes (830 to 915 PM MST). ||This is a list of the damage: ||Homes destroyed - 15|Major damage - 25|Minor damage - 17|Affected - 10|Impacted - 53||Total:   120||Most of the homes that were damaged were in Mayer with a few in Spring Valley.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm produced an estimated 2-3 foot rise in the Dinnebito Wash at Navajo Route 41. Time is approximate.
Heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar caused Big Bug Creek to flash flood in Meyer. The waster rose 2 to 2.5 feet (50 feet wide) at the Central Avenue Bridge.
Cedar Creek rose 8 feet at the Highway 73 Bridge after a thunderstorm dropped heavy rain over the Cedar Fire scar (June  2016).

Strong thunderstorm winds snapped a tree trunk greater than 12 inches in diameter in front of the Clemenceau Heritage Museum. The thunderstorm also produced penny sized hail and over an inch of rain in 30 minutes.
A thunderstorm over Williams produce 1.37 inches of rain in 40 minutes, very gusty winds, and lots of lightning. Moderate street flooding was observed in the neighborhood southwest of Downtown.
A thunderstorm began producing heavy rain in the Payson area by 419 PM MST. A spotter measured 1.10 inches of rain in 45 minutes. The street and neighbor's front yard flooded with no damage.
Heavy rain over the Cedar Fire scar produced flash flooding in Carrizo Creek. The river gauge at Carrizo peak rose to 10 feet (215 PM MST). The creek was back down to 5 feet by 330 PM MST.
Heavy rain over the Cedar Fire scar caused flash flooding in Cedar Creek. The gauge at Highway 73 peaked at 6 feet and was receding at 300 PM MST.

A wet microburst produced high winds at the Prescott Airport (Love Field). The peak wind gust was 68 MPH at 325 PM MST.  A few aircraft were moved/turned by the wind. No damage was reported. Strong winds were observed for 30 minutes.
A thunderstorm produced 1.67 inches of rain in one hour just north of McNary.

A trained spotter reported a strong thunderstorm with one inch of rain in 30 to 45 minutes, wind gusts to 47 MPH, and pea sized hail. There was minor flooding with a lot of rocks, debris, and tree branches on Page Springs Road.
Dry Beaver Creek rose from 0.95 feet at 330 PM to 3.74 feet at 445 PM. The creek then slowly decreased through the evening.
Heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar caused flash flooding downstream. The water was reported to be two feet over the Spring Lane Bridge crossing Big Bug Creek.
The Agua Fria River near Humboldt rose from 1.46 feet to 4.12 feet in about an hour.
The Verde River near Camp Verde rose from 4.01 feet at 345 PM MST to 10.39 feet at  445 PM MST. The fastest rate of rise was from 6.25 feet to 10.39 feet from 430 PM to 445 PM MST.

A thunderstorm produced 1.46 inches of rain in a short time (most of that was in less than an hour). The visibility dropped to less than a quarter mile. The ditches were running level with the road. The wash behind the spotter's house was running full (dept unknown). Eight inches of water accumulated in the back yard. The event was around 45 minutes long.
A thunderstorm produced a wind gust of 60 MPH at the Sedona Airport.  Heavy rain (0.89 in under an hour) dropped the visibility down to half a mile.

Black Canyon River was flowing three to four feet deep across Maren Avenue (a low water crossing). The water came up there around 930 PM MST. A second wave of water was recorded on a river gauge (AFRA3) just down stream. This gauge went from 5.26 feet to 10.40 feet in just 15 minutes (that is an increase from 449 CFS to 3,545 CFS).
Wind gusts from a thunderstorm (estimated at 50 MPH) damaged trees and an awning at an RV park in Camp Verde.
Four or five low water crossings were flooded on Indian Route 15 between Cornfields and Highway 77. All crossings were passable.
Chinle Police received a report of water flowing across a road near Tselani and Cottonwood at 330 PM MST.

Heavy rain over Utah caused flash flooding in Paria Canyon that flowed into Arizona. The River gauge on the Paria River (just before the confluence with the Colorado River near Lees Ferry) showed at 2 foot rise (6.16 foot stage).

Heavy rain fell over the Cedar Fire scar and produced flash flooding. The White  Mountain  Apache Emergency Manager observed 5 feet of water in Cedar Creek with a notable  in just 10 minutes. Carrizo Creek had 2.5 feet of water flowing.
Arizona Department of Public Safety reported 6 inches of water across State Route 377 at milepost 12.8.
Quarter sized (one inch diameter) hail was reported from a thunderstorm in southeast Sedona.  The storm also produced 0.75 inches of rain.
A Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS) reported a 59 MPH wind gust.
Around 0.75 inches of rain fell in 30 minutes.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain over the Prescott area. At one point, the rainfall rate was 9.22 inches per hour! It rained  1.89 inches in one hour.
The Yavapai Flood District Office reported one foot of water over area roads due to the heavy rain.
The river gauge at Martinez Wash rose 2.2 feet (1730 CFS) due to heavy rain upstream.
A thunderstorm with heavy rain produced flowing water in Lower Antelope Canyon. Tours were cancelled for the day.

The USGS river gauge on Granite Creek in Prescott rose 4.42 feet in 30 minutes (11:15 AM to 11:45 AM MST). ||A trained spotter reported ponding and running water in streets near Yavapai College. Pea sized hail (1/4 inch) fell for 15 minutes.
Two inches of rain fell near Yava.  West Eastwood Wash was flowing over a low water crossing eight to ten inches deep and 150 feet wide. The heavy rain lasted for two hours.
Heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar caused a flash flood in Big Bug Creek  The river gauge at State Route 69 reported a peak of 5.1 feet...an estimated four foot rise.
The Sedona Fire Department could not respond to an emergency call due to water flowing over Verde Valley School Road. At least two feet of water was flowing over the road.
Beaver Creek Road was impassible due to flash flooding at School Hose Wash.
The stream gauge on Beaver Creek (2 SW McGuireville) showed a sudden rise of three feet.
An inch and a half of rain caused minor street flooding in the Sedona Shadows Neighborhood.

At 10:52 AM MST, the Prescott Airport reported a funnel cloud three miles northeast of the tower moving northeast. At 11:25 AM MST, they reported that the cell was weakening with just a moderate intensity rain shaft. The duration of the funnel cloud was 15 minutes.

Heavy rain in Utah created a flash flood that flowed through the Paria River from Utah to the Colorado River in Arizona. The stream gauge near the Colorado River indicated a two foot rise in the normally dry river bed.
A thunderstorm produced heavy rain over the Goodwin Fire scar that caused flash flooding on the Agua Fria River. The stream gauge went from 1 foot to 4.91 feet during the flash flood.

A flash flood was reported at Shadow Rim Girl Scout Camp. Chase Creek was six to eight feet deep and over the banks. Water lines were damaged and roads were washed out. They received 2.45 inches of rain at the camp. Flash flooding was reported in the East Verde River at the Water Wheel (near Houston Mesa Road). That road was impassable from water and heavy debris in that location. The The East Verde River upstream was flowing five to six feet deep.  A weather spotter claimed that it was the worst flooding in many years.
The Arizona Department of Transportation reported that Highway 163 north of Kayenta was flooded between Mile Posts 399 and 400.
A thunderstorm produced 1.60 inches of rain in 45 minutes (heavy rain still falling a the time of the report). Water was starting to run in the normally dry washes.
The river gauge on Beaver Creek at Montezuma Castle rose 3.36 feet in 90 minutes.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain across portions of the Verde Valley.  A four inch bird bath was filled to over flowing in 90 minutes just north of McGuireville. Water flooded their back yard and two inches of water was flowing over their road.  A spotter reported 1.90 inches of rain in Cornville. Sand and gravel washed over their road as well.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain (2.25-2.49 inches) and pea sized hail (1/4-1/2 inch diameter) over a two hour period.
A thunderstorm produced heavy rain and a flash flood that the Supai Police tracked as it moved down through Havasu Creek. The river gauge near the Village of Supai rose around 2 feet.
A thunderstorm produced quarter sized (1 inch in diameter) hail with very heavy rain. Some stones were larger.
Cottonwood Police Department reported flooding in homes in several areas in Cottonwood.
Wind gusts to around 50 MPH broke small tree branches (less than 2 inches in diameter). The winds also produced blowing dust that reduced the visibility.
High winds from a thunderstorm knocked down power lines on Sycamore Canyon Road near Tuzigoot National Monument.
A thunderstorm with heavy rain caused a flash flood in the normally dry Dry Silver Creek Wash. A video submitted by weather spotter showed the water to be around six feet deep.
Thunderstorms with heavy rain washed mud and rocks over Navajo Route 15 between Greasewood and Ganado.

A thunderstorm produce damaging winds in the Page area.  The hanger at the Page Airport was damaged. The Jet Center windows were blown out by the winds. A few trees were uprooted. The Page ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 56 MPH at 1238 PM MST.  ||Multiple homes in the Champan Village area were damaged by flying debris and falling trees. Two power poles were destroyed when wind blown trees fell on them. This caused power outages in the area.
Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused flash flooding in the Paria River. The USGS gauge on the Paria River near Lees Ferry rose over four feet to over 1500 CFS.
A 59-year-old man from Cottonwood drowned around 6:30am while attempting to cross Beaver Creek at Reay Road in Rimrock.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN APACHE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The ASOS at the St Johns Airport measured a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 240 AM MST.  Wind gusts of 40 MPH or higher were observed from around midnight to 500 AM MST. The peak wind gust at the Springerville Airport was 75 MPH at 655 AM MST. The wind gusted over 60 MPH from 1030 PM on the 20th to around 1240 PM MST on the 21st.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN COCONINO COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The ADOT wind sensor at Two Guns measured a peak wind gust of 62 MPH at 853 PM MST.  Wind gusts of 50 MPH or greater were observed from around 815 to around 11 PM MST.

A human caused fire started just after 1230 PM about 20 miles north of Flagstaff in grassland. A drone caught fire when it landed in grass. The fire quickly spread to around 50 acres by the time firefighters arrived on scene. Firefighters were able to burn out around the Chapel of the Holy Dove to prevent any damage to the historic landmark.  Coconino National Forest firefighters and Summit Fire Department contained the Kendrick Fire at 335 acres by late afternoon. ADOT used a pilot car to usher traffic on Highway 180 through the thick smoke impacting visibility.
Heavy rain (about half an inch in an hour) was a contributing factor to a five-vehicle collision involving fatalities and additional injuries on southbound Interstate 17 at State Route 169.

Flagstaff received 5 inches of snow, Williams received 6 inches of snow, and Bellemont received 6.8 inches of snow.  Local schools were on a two hour delay. There were several slide-offs and non-injury crashes on Flagstaff area roads. Fourteen inches of snow fell at 10,800 feet elevation.
Interstate 40 was closed for several hours just east of Ash Fork due to icy roads, steep grades, and crashes.
A trained spotter in Forest Lakes reported 11 inches of snow in 11 hours.

The Flagstaff Airport received 8.5 inches of snow.  Other areas from Munds Park to Flagstaff received 7 to 9 inches of snow. Flagstaff area school had their first snow day of the season. Coconino County and Flagstaff City offices opened two hours late because of the snow.
A trained spotter reported a peak wind gust of 61 MPH three miles south of Prescott Valley.
The wind gusted over 60 MPH from around midnight until after 630 AM. The peak wind gust was 75 MPH at 619 AM.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN COCONINO COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The wind sensor at Two Guns had wind gusts over 58 MPH from around 440 to 640 AM MST. The peak wind gust was 64 MPH at 515 AM MST.
The wind sensor at Limestone Canyon reported wind gusts above 58 MPH between 630 to around 1130 AM. The peak wind gust was 64 MPH at 924 MPH.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN NAVAJO COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The Winslow ASOS reported wind gusts over 58 MPH between 140 PM to 310 PM. The peak wind gust was 64 MPH at 305 PM. Petrified Forest National Monument reported a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 1223 PM.

The Flagstaff Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 59 MPH wind at 11:18 AM.  Several ponderosa pine trees were blown over in Sunset Crater National Monument. A local ski resort (9,000 to 11,500 feet) was closed all day because of the high winds.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN APACHE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: St Johns Airport reported wind gusts of 58 MPH or higher from 1245 PM to 200 PM. The peak wind gust was 63 MPH at 1254 PM. Petrified Forest National Monument reported a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 1223 PM.  The wind sensor in Lupton reported a peak wind gust of 65 MPH at 0343 PM. The peak wind gust at Springerville Airport was 72 MPH at 1120 AM.
The Window Rock ASOS reported wind gusts over 58 MPH from around 330 PM to 420 PM. The peak wind gust was 62 MPH at 410 PM.
The wind sensor in Kykotsmovi Village reported a peak wind gust of 63 MPH at 1213 PM.

events.cz_name: NORTHEAST PLATEAUS AND MESAS SOUTH OF HIGHWAY 264
events.event_narrative: The wind sensor in Kykotsmovi Village reported a peak wind gust of 63 MPH at 1213 PM.
A wind sensor in Heber-Overgaard reported a 72 MPH wind gust at 213 PM.
Just over eight (8.1) inches of snow was reported in central Flagstaff.  Other reports in the area ranged from  5 to 7 inches in Munds Park, Flagstaff, and Williams.

Five inches of new snow fell overnight in Fredonia at around 4700 feet elevation. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon at 8,000 feet elevation only received 4.8 inches of snow.
An ADOT wind sensor in Lupton (along I-40) recorded a peak wind gust of 61 MPH at 843  AM MST.

The winds were sustained over 40 MPH from 1230 PM to 215 PM.

events.event_narrative: The ADOT wind sensor at Two Guns along Interstate 40 had a peak wind gust of 62 MPH. The time of the high winds for this zone was estimated by using the Winslow ASOS times (just 5 miles across the zone boundary).
The Bright Angel RAWS station (8134 ft) reported a peak wind gust of 58 MPH at 1107 PM.
The ASOS at Show Low Airport reported a peak wind gust of 59 MPH at 1135 AM.  The sustain wind was over 40 MPH at times between 930 AM and 515 PM.
The peak wind gust at Limestone Canyon (RAWS) was 63 MPH at 324 PM.  The winds gusted over 58 MPH between 100 PM and 430 PM. The peak wind gust at Heber-Overgaard was 61 MPH at 1235 PM.
The RAWS 4 miles north of House Rock reported a peak wind of 60 MPH at 319 AM.

The peak wind gust at Window Rock Airport was 66 MPH 254 PM. Blowing dust/sand reduced the visibility below 3 miles between 1225 PM and 500 PM. The visibility dropped down to a mile at around 300 PM. The ASOS stopped transmitting just after 335 PM. The peak wind gust at Lupton was 66 MPH at 233 PM. The winds gusted over 58 MPH between 150 PM and  345 PM. The Navajo Times Newspaper reported that a roof was blown off a mobile home in Kinlichee (7 miles northeast of Ganado) at 339 PM.

events.event_narrative: The ADOT wind sensor at Two Guns reported a peak wind gust of 59 MPH at 723 PM on April 16.

The Mesonet station 4 miles north of House Rock (Four Springs RAWS) reported a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 119 AM on April 17th.  Paria Point RAWS (7235 feet) reported a peak wind gust of 62 MPH a 1100 PM.

events.cz_name: LITTLE COLORADO RIVER VALLEY IN APACHE COUNTY
events.event_narrative: The peak wind gust at Springerville Airport ASOS was 73 MPH at 735 AM. The AWOS  at the airport had a peak wind gust of 76 MPH at 655 AM. The wind gusted over 58 MPH from 1135 PM to 1120 AM on the 17th. The sustained winds were above 40 MPH for much of the time between and 1130 PM and 120 PM. The sustained winds in St Johns was above 40 MPH for much of the time between 720 AM and 1115 AM.  The wind gusts were above 58 MPH from 735 AM to 900 AM with a peak wind gust of 69 MPH at 743 AM. Power and phone lines were reported blown down in St Johns and Springerville between 805 and 809 AM. The Concho RAWS reported wind gusts of 58 MPH or higher from 800 AM to 915 AM with a peak wind gust of 59 MPH at 854 AM.

The Tinder Fire was first seen by Moqui Tower lookout on April 27 11:43 AM.  Investigators determined that the fire originated in the East Clear Creek drainage approximately 1 mile downstream from Forest Road 95. Forest Road 95 runs north-south and is located approximately 1.5 miles east of C.C. Cragin (Blue Ridge) Reservoir. The cause of the fire was an abandoned illegal campfire. The fire burned 16,309 acres, 33 primary residences, and 54 minor structures.

Investigators determined that the fire originated in the East Clear Creek drainage approximately 1 mile downstream from Forest Road 95. Forest Road 95 runs north-south and is located approximately 1.5 miles east of C.C. Cragin (Blue Ridge) Reservoir. The cause of the fire was an abandoned illegal campfire. The fire burned 16,309 acres, 33 primary residences, and 54 minor structures.

The RAWS at Limestone Canyon showed that the wind gusted over 40 MPH from around 620 AM to 850 AM.  The peak wind gust was 61 MPH at 824 AM. An ADOT wind sensor at the junction of SR-277 and SR-377 had a peak wind gust of 61 MPH at 923 AM. The winds gusted over 58 MPH between 920 AM and 1000 AM.
The peak wind gust at the Greer RAWS was 59 MPH at 0835 AM. The peak wind gust at the Show Low Airport was 58 MPH at 855 AM and 955 AM.

The sustained winds were above 40 MPH between 1120 AM to 210 PM MST. The St Johns Airport reported a peak wind gust of 58 MPH at 337 PM MST. The sustained winds were 40 MPH or higher at times between 300 and 400 PM MST.

The Winslow Airport ASOS recorded a peak wind gust of 63 MPH at 105 PM MST.  The sustained winds were 40 MPH or higher much of the time between 1250 AM and 240 PM MST. The ADOT wind sensor on Highway 77 near Concho had sustained winds above 40 MPH from 1250 PM until 315 PM.  The peak wind gust was 58 MPH at 213 PM.

The Limestone RAWS reported a peak wind gust of 71 MPH at 324 PM MST. The sustained winds were above 40 MPH between around 100 PM MST and 400 PM MST. Mesonet stations around Heber-Overgaard reported wind gusts of 60 and 61 MPH between 1013 AM and 1053 AM.

The Grand Canyon Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 303 PM MST.
A funnel cloud was reported east of Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.
The Window Rock Airport had a peak wind gust of 59 MPH at 1251 PM MST.
The Flagstaff Airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 60 MPH at 243 PM.

events.event_narrative: The Springerville Airport reported a peak wind gust of 61 MPH at 115 PM MST.
Heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused street flooding in Taylor including Paper Mill Road and West Willow Lane.
Wind from a thunderstorm broke a power pole at Highway 89 and Road 4 North.
Heavy rain fell from 200 PM to 240 PM MST near Young. A rain gauge measured 1.10 inches of rain in 40 minutes.
The AWOS at the Sedona Airport reported a peak wind gust of 64 MPH.
The Yavapai Flood Control gauge at Perkinsville reported at least a 2.28 foot rise on the Verde River downstream from a thunderstorm that produced heavy rain.
